abstract: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis has been implicated in learning and memory. Although increasing neurogenesis has been associated with improved spatial learning and pattern discrimination, whether these benefits differ between male and female mice remains unclear. The goal of this study was to see if increasing adult hippocampal neurogenesis improves learning in male and female mice, and whether the benefit is the same in both sexes. We used conditional deletion of the pro-apoptotic gene Bax to increase the survival of newborn dentate granule cells. Male and female BAX knockout (KO) and wild-type (WT) mice were tested in Intellicage place learning and reversal learning tasks, and an A/B context discrimination task. BAX KO mice had more tdTomato-positive newborn dentate granule cells than BAX WT mice, with no significant effect of sex. During Intellicage adaptation, there were no differences between genotypes or sexes in total visits and licks. During place learning, male mice had a higher percent correct response than female mice, while female mice showed increases in licks and correct visits from day 1 to day 4. BAX KO mice made more visits overall but had a lower percent correct response than BAX WT mice on day 4. During reversal learning, male BAX KO mice showed a decrease in visits and had fewer visits with a lick than male BAX WT mice on day 4. In the A/B task, male BAX KO mice had higher discrimination scores than male BAX WT mice on day 5, while female BAX KO mice showed an initial advantage over female BAX WT mice. These results partially support our hypothesis that increasing neurogenesis would benefit male mice more. Overall, increasing the survival of newborn dentate granule cells does not improve learning in the same way across sexes and tasks.
